size_t binary_search( int *data, size_t N, int value ) { 
size_t lo = 0, hi = N - 1; 
while( lo < hi ) { 
size_t mid = lo + ( hi - lo ) / 2; 
if( data[mid] < value ) { 
lo = mid + 1; 
} else { 
hi = mid; 
} 
} 
return ( hi == lo && data[lo] == value ) ? lo : N; 
}

Content: MIT 2014 — Week 1

Lectures: 3 sessions / week; 2 hrs / session

Course Description
Do you want to learn how create blazing fast programs, be organized about developing a software project, write C/C++ code that will keep the people who maintain it very happy, learn how to ace an interview in either of these languages since you’ll know them so well, and understand how to properly debug your code when you inevitably run into problems? Then this might be the crash course for you.
This course is a fast-paced introduction to the C and C++ programming languages, both of which are useful for classes, research, and jobs. Focus will be placed on practical knowledge, especially best practices, the powerful advantages C/C++ can offer, and modern features of C++. Students will come away with an understanding of when and why you might want to use C/C++ over another language, how both “low-level” and more abstracted programming can help you, and how to best develop your own software projects in these languages. This course assumes no C/C++ knowledge, but is intended for programmers with some background and experience in other languages.
Because this course is offered during IAP

Do you want to learn how create blazing fast programs, be organized about developing a software project, write C/C++ code that will keep the people who maintain it very happy, learn how to ace an interview in either of these languages since you’ll know them so well, and understand how to properly debug your code when you inevitably run into problems? [Guidelines]
Content: [F: Functions]
Rule F.16: F.16: For “in” parameters, pass cheaply-copied types by value and others by reference to const
Reason: Both let the caller know that a function will not modify the argument, and both allow initialization by rvalues.
What is “cheap to copy” depends on the machine architecture, but two or three words (doubles, pointers, references) are usually best passed by value.
When copying is cheap, nothing beats the simplicity and safety of copying, and for small objects (up to two or three words) it is also faster than passing by reference because it does not require an extra indirection to access from the function.

 dest = src;
}

Content: [P: Philosophy] Rule P.5: P.5: Prefer compile-time checking to run-time checking
Example: // Int is an alias used for integers
int bits = 0; // don't: avoidable code
for (Int i = 1; i; i <<= 1)
 ++bits;
if (bits < 32)
 cerr << "Int too small\n";
This example fails to achieve what it is trying to achieve (because overflow is undefined) and should be replaced with a simple 
static_assert
:
// Int is an alias used for integers
static_assert(sizeof(Int) >= 4); // do: compile-time check
Or better still just use the type system and replace 
Int
 with 
int32_t
.
```cpp
// Int is an alias used for integers
int bits = 0;         // don't: avoidable code
for (Int i = 1; i; i <<= 1)
    ++bits;
if (bits < 32)
    cerr << "Int too small\n";

// Int is an alias used for integers
static_assert(sizeof(Int) >= 4);    // do: compile-time check
```

Based on the retrieved documentation, `std::condition_variable` provides a default constructor that takes no parameters and constructs the object ready for use [1](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/thread/condition_variable).

The three key member functions you will need are:

- **`wait(lock, predicate)`** — atomically releases the lock and suspends the thread until the predicate returns `true`
- **`notify_one()`** — wakes up one waiting thread
- **`notify_all()`** — wakes up all waiting threads

The lock passed to `wait()` must be a `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>`, which is precisely why `std::lock_guard` cannot be used with a condition variable.

For the full formal specification, cppreference is your most reliable source: [1](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/thread/condition_variable)

The standard pattern for `std::condition_variable::wait()` requires that the consumer already holds the lock **before** calling `wait()`. The reason is subtle but important: `wait()` must **atomically** release the lock and suspend the thread. If the unlock and the sleep were two separate steps, the producer could sneak in and call `notify_one()` in between — and the consumer would sleep forever, missing the notification entirely. This is called a **spurious wakeup / lost wakeup** race.

The idiomatic C++ solution is `std::unique_lock` (not `std::lock_guard`), because `wait()` requires a lock it can release and re-acquire internally.

So the corrected consumer sequence is:

1. Acquire `std::unique_lock`
2. Call `cv.wait(lock, predicate)` — this atomically releases the lock and blocks
3. On notification, the lock is **automatically re-acquired** before your thread resumes
4. Walk the cart, collect totals
5. Release the lock, then print

**[ANALOGY_SCAFFOLD]**

Think of a condition variable like a waiting room at a doctor's office. A patient (thread) enters the waiting room only after checking in at the front desk — that is, after acquiring a lock. When the nurse calls them (the condition variable is notified), the patient must re-check with the front desk before proceeding into the exam room.

The critical detail is this: while the patient is sitting and waiting, they must be able to **temporarily release** their hold on the front desk so other patients can check in. This is exactly what `std::unique_lock` enables that `std::lock_guard` does not — it supports being unlocked and re-locked mid-scope. A condition variable's `wait()` call requires this ability to atomically release the lock during the wait and reacquire it upon waking.

This is why `std::condition_variable` in the C++ standard library is designed to work specifically with `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>`.

Now, a guiding question to deepen your understanding: given that `std::unique_lock` can be released mid-scope, what do you think would go wrong if the lock were simply dropped permanently rather than atomically paired with the wait?

[Syllabus]
Content: MIT 2014 — Week 1
Course Meeting Times
Lectures: 3 sessions / week; 2 hrs / session
Open Labs: 1 session / week; 2 hrs / session
Course Description
Do you want to learn how create blazing fast programs, be organized about developing a software project, write C/C++ code that will keep the people who maintain it very happy, learn how to ace an interview in either of these languages since you’ll know them so well, and understand how to properly debug your code when you inevitably run into problems? Then this might be the crash course for you.
This course is a fast-paced introduction to the C and C++ programming languages, both of which are useful for classes, research, and jobs. Focus will be placed on practical knowledge, especially best practices, the powerful advantages C/C++ can offer, and modern features of C++. Students will come away with an understanding of when and why you might want to use C/C++ over another language, how both “low-level” and more abstracted programming can help you, and how to best develop your own software projects in these languages. This course assumes no C/C++ knowledge, but is intended for programmers with some background and experience in other languages.
Because this course is offered during IAP
, lectures are given on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays. There are open lab hours offered on Wednesday evenings for those who seek assistance, though attendance during this time is not required.

Content: [Lecture1.pdf p.18] Memory Model 
Pointers 
How do you get at this information about memory? 
Through pointers; that is, the & and * operators 
int a = 5; The address of a is &a.

Content: [P: Philosophy] Rule P.5: P.5: Prefer compile-time checking to run-time checking
Example: // Int is an alias used for integers
int bits = 0; // don't: avoidable code
for (Int i = 1; i; i <<= 1)
 ++bits;
if (bits < 32)
 cerr << "Int too small\n";
This example fails to achieve what it is trying to achieve (because overflow is undefined) and should be replaced with a simple 
static_assert
:
// Int is an alias used for integers
static_assert(sizeof(Int) >= 4); // do: compile-time check
Or better still just use the type system and replace 
Int
 with 
int32_t
.
```cpp
// Int is an alias used for integers
int bits = 0;         // don't: avoidable code
for (Int i = 1; i; i <<= 1)
    ++bits;
if (bits < 32)
    cerr << "Int too small\n";

// Int is an alias used for integers
static_assert(sizeof(Int) >= 4);    // do: compile-time check
```

Content: [ES: Expressions and statements] Rule ES.107: ES.107: Don’t use unsigned for subscripts, prefer gsl::index
Example, bad: vector<int> vec = /*...*/;

for (int i = 0; i < vec.size(); i += 2) // might not be big enough
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (unsigned i = 0; i < vec.size(); i += 2) // risk wraparound
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (auto i = 0; i < vec.size(); i += 2) // might not be big enough
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (vector<int>::size_type i = 0; i < vec.size(); i += 2) // verbose
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (auto i = vec.size()-1; i >= 0; i -= 2) // bug
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
for (int i = vec.size()-1; i >= 0; i -= 2) // might not be big enough
 cout << vec[i] << '\n';
